intro.title: Explore Los Dos Templos
intro.description: Los Dos Templos is located in Guadalajara, Jalisco, Mexico. It consists of two exceptionally well-preserved 17th and 18th-century magnificent churches that are still in use today. They once belonged to a vast convent complex and are now separated by the beautiful and peaceful Jardín de San Francisco, making it a perfect place to experience Mexican Baroque architectural art.

alsoKnownAs.title: Highlights
items: Templo de San Francisco de Asís: One of the oldest churches in Guadalajara with a solemn and classic exterior.
Templo de Nuestra Señora de Aránzazu: Highly recommended! The only church in the city retaining three complete 18th-century Churrigueresque (Ultra-Baroque) gilded wooden altars.
Jardín de San Francisco: A beautiful and tranquil square separating the two churches, perfect for visitors to rest.
Prime Location: Located in the historic center of Guadalajara, Jalisco, easily accessible.

intro.welcome: Welcome to **Los Dos Templos**, whose name translates from Spanish as the **Two Temples**, widely recognized as one of the central historic landmarks of **Guadalajara**. Located in the heart of **Guadalajara**, **Jalisco**, **Mexico**, this destination serves as a primary hub for travelers visiting the region.
intro.nearbyHeading: Landmarks & Attractions Around Los Dos Templos
intro.nearby: When visiting **Los Dos Templos**, visitors can easily explore surrounding historical landmarks and points of interest, including **Catedral de Guadalajara** and **Teatro Degollado**.

route.title: Tour Route
route.overview: Discover the ideal route to explore Los Dos Templos and experience the essence of Baroque architectural art and Mexican history.
steps: Arrive at Templo de San Francisco de Asís in the morning to admire its solemn exterior and long history.
Walk through the beautiful and peaceful Jardín de San Francisco and take a short break in the square.
Focus your visit on Templo de Nuestra Señora de Aránzazu to admire its stunning 18th-century Churrigueresque gilded wooden altars.
After the visit, walk to the Guadalajara historic center to explore other attractions or enjoy local cuisine.
supplements: Please prepare some cash for buying souvenirs or snacks nearby.
Please keep quiet inside the churches and respect local religious customs.
When photographing the gilded altars, please avoid using flash so as not to disturb others.

sections.title: Historical Significance
sections.content: Los Dos Templos is an important historical and cultural landmark in Guadalajara. These two churches once belonged to a massive convent complex, witnessing centuries of urban evolution, and serve as an important place to understand Mexican religion and history.

sections.title: Cultural Landscape
sections.content: Templo de Nuestra Señora de Aránzazu is the only church in the city that retains three complete 18th-century Churrigueresque (Ultra-Baroque) gilded wooden altars. Its visual impact is truly breathtaking.

sections.title: Visiting Experience
sections.content: Stroll through the Jardín de San Francisco between the two churches and feel the peaceful atmosphere. It is an unforgettable architectural and cultural experience, allowing you to closely feel the depth and charm of Mexican history.

transport.transitTitle: Which bus routes reach Los Dos Templos?
transport.transitIntro: City buses running along Av. 16 de Septiembre and Calzada Revolución stop almost right outside the site. The stop in the area is known as “Dos Templos” or “San Francisco”.

T15 — a main city bus line passing through downtown Guadalajara.
Ruta 86 — another frequent option around the historic center.

officialManagement.title: About Los Dos Templos
officialManagement.text: Los Dos Templos are famous historic churches in Guadalajara, consisting of Templo de San Francisco de Asís and Templo de Nuestra Señora de Aránzazu, carrying rich architectural and cultural value.

historyTimeline.title: History & Significance of Los Dos Templos

items.title: Colonial Period: Foundation
items.description: Los Dos Templos was built during the Mexican colonial period and originally belonged to a massive convent complex. Templo de San Francisco de Asís is one of the oldest churches in Guadalajara, featuring a solemn exterior.

items.title: 18th Century: Baroque Pinnacle
items.description: Templo de Nuestra Señora de Aránzazu shone brightly during this period, with three complete Churrigueresque (Ultra-Baroque) gilded wooden altars built inside, becoming a gem of Mexican architectural art.

items.title: 20th Century: Urban Evolution
items.description: With the urban development of Guadalajara, the original convent complex underwent changes. Today, the two churches are separated by the beautiful and peaceful Jardín de San Francisco, serving as a resting square for citizens and tourists.

items.title: 21st Century: Cultural Tourism Destination
items.description: In the 21st century, Los Dos Templos attracts more and more visitors with its well-preserved centuries-old church architecture and stunning gilded altars, becoming an important window to experience Mexican history and art.

historyTimeline.guideContent: When visiting, you can start with **Templo de San Francisco de Asís** to feel its solemnity; then take a break at **Jardín de San Francisco**; next, focus on visiting **Templo de Nuestra Señora de Aránzazu** to admire the breathtaking Churrigueresque gilded altars; finally, stroll through the historic center to deeply understand the important position of these monuments in Mexican history.

faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions about Los Dos Templos

items.q: Where is Los Dos Templos located?
items.a: Los Dos Templos is located in the historic center of Guadalajara, at Av. 16 de Septiembre & Calz. Revolución, Zona Centro, 44100 Guadalajara, Jalisco, Mexico.

items.q: Which two churches form Los Dos Templos?
items.a: Los Dos Templos is formed by two historic churches: Templo de San Francisco de Asís and Templo de Nuestra Señora de Aránzazu. They once belonged to a vast convent complex and are now separated by the peaceful Jardín de San Francisco.

items.q: Is Los Dos Templos free to visit?
items.a: Yes, visiting Los Dos Templos and entering its two churches is free of charge. As a public historic landmark of Guadalajara, it is open to visitors free of charge year-round.

items.q: What are the opening hours of Los Dos Templos?
items.a: The churches are generally open throughout the day, and daytime visits are recommended for the best light and atmosphere. Please verify the latest official schedule before your visit.

items.q: What can I see at Los Dos Templos?
items.a: Visitors can admire the colonial Baroque architecture of the two churches, especially the three complete 18th-century Churrigueresque (Ultra-Baroque) gilded wooden altars preserved inside the Templo de Nuestra Señora de Aránzazu, as well as the tranquil Jardín de San Francisco.

items.q: How do I get to Los Dos Templos in Guadalajara?
items.a: Los Dos Templos is located in the historic center of Guadalajara. You can take Line 3 (Línea 3) of the Guadalajara light rail (Tren Ligero) to Guadalajara Centro station and walk, or reach it on foot or by taxi from the city center.

items.q: Which landmarks are near Los Dos Templos?
items.a: While visiting Los Dos Templos, you can also explore nearby landmarks such as Catedral de Guadalajara (Guadalajara Cathedral) and Teatro Degollado, both just a short walk away in the historic center.

items.q: Which is the oldest church in Guadalajara?
items.a: The Templo de San Francisco de Asís, part of Los Dos Templos, is one of the oldest religious buildings still standing in the historic center: the current church was built between the 17th and 18th centuries on the site of the original Franciscan convent.

items.q: Are Los Dos Templos Gothic in style?
items.a: Not exactly: Los Dos Templos showcase Mexican colonial Baroque, including the gilded Churrigueresque altars inside the Templo de Nuestra Señora de Aránzazu. If you are looking for Gothic architecture in Guadalajara, the best-known example is the neo-Gothic towers of the Cathedral, added in the mid-19th century.

items.q: Which bus takes me to Los Dos Templos?
items.a: Several city buses run along Av. 16 de Septiembre and Calzada Revolución, including Ruta 231, T15 and Ruta 86; the stop in the area is known as “Dos Templos”, so ask the driver to let you know. You can also take Line 3 of the Tren Ligero to Guadalajara Centro station and walk a few minutes.

itineraries.title: Recommended Visit Plans
itineraries.intro: Neutral reference plans, not commercial promotions. Mix them to fit your time and mobility.

halfDay.title: Classic Half-Day Route (2–3 h)
steps: Start inside the church of Nuestra Señora de Aranzazú and admire its 18th-century gilded altars.
Rest at Jardín de San Francisco between the two churches and enjoy the facing views.
Continue to San Francisco church to appreciate its sober, historic atmosphere.
If time allows, stroll along Avenida 16 de Septiembre toward the historic center squares.

fullDay.title: Full-Day Deep Route (5–6 h)
steps: Morning: follow the half-day route to complete both churches and the garden.
Lunch: pick from general market-style food areas in the historic center (type reference only, no brands).
Afternoon: walk the historic center axis to public landmarks (Cathedral, Plaza de Armas, Teatro Degollado).
Optional: step into a nearby public cultural venue for an indoor break.
Dusk: return to Jardín de San Francisco to see the lit facades.

itineraries.crowdNote: Choose by your group mix and preferred pace.

crowdItems.title: Families with children
points: The garden and squares offer open space to rest; keep lawns and benches clean.
Inside the churches keep quiet and explain visiting manners to kids.
Public toilets and common food types are nearby; bring water and wipes.
Avoid Mass hours for a smoother visit.

crowdItems.title: Photography & architecture
points: Side light in the early morning and late afternoon flatters facades and the garden.
No flash inside or in front of the gilded altars.
Frame street-level views from the corners; cross streets carefully.
After dusk, lit facades and the plaza are great for night shots.

crowdItems.title: Low effort / accessible
points: The main visit follows flat sidewalks, and the garden has benches to rest.
Some historic interiors have steps; prioritize outdoor areas and ask staff to confirm accessible routes.
Watch for public and accessible restroom signage along the way.
To avoid crowds, arrive before 10:00.

blocks.title: Architecture & culture quick guide
points: Churrigueresque is an 18th-century ultra-Baroque style known for richly carved, gilded altarpieces.
The two churches once belonged to one large convent complex; the garden now separates them, and both witness the city’s religious and public life.
Much of the interior art was made by local artisans, reflecting cultural exchange between Europe and the Americas.
Look at altars, timber structures and towers: they are clues for dating a historic building.

blocks.title: Etiquette in religious spaces
points: These are working churches: keep quiet and silence your phone.
Do not walk across the sanctuary or interrupt services during Mass.
Turn off flash when photographing interiors and altars; respect no-photo zones.
Dress modestly when entering the interiors.

blocks.title: Responsibility & safety
points: Do not climb, lean on or touch monuments, sculptures or railings.
The garden and squares are public: take your litter and care for green areas and benches.
Watch your belongings during busy days and crowds.
Ask permission before photographing people, and respect worshippers and locals.
In an emergency call 911 or ask nearby staff for help.

historyExtra.legendText: Guadalajara residents commonly use “los dos templos” (the two churches) to orient people in this area — a short, familiar label also used by transport, taxis and maps. Two churches of different styles facing each other across a garden have become part of the neighborhood’s collective memory and a natural meeting point for walking tours.
